en: As though fashioned in its likeness;
His very scalp matched his father’s scalp,
As though one had been fitted over the other.
Broad-mouthed and cliff-browed,
His upper lip jutted wide
Like a Kalmyk’s bag.
His lashes were flame, his eyes were embers;
No mortal ever held such wonder.
His beauty was singular, his gaze direct;
Among the multitude, his speech was forthright.
His brows were dense as thickets;
The formidable pale boy
Looked able to swallow alive anyone who grappled with him.
He was like a champion who ruled a nation;
God Most High fashions
His servants in every manner.
If he gathered himself and sprang,
He looked ready truly to conquer the foe.
His brow was high, his menace fierce;
He would flatten anyone who challenged him.
Seeing the boy’s valor,
Abandon hope of a peaceful end.
His stature and bearing were extraordinary;
From afar, he looked like a mountain.
He had been named Seytek,
And from his mother’s words he learned
That his people were the Kyrgyz,
That renowned Talas was their land,
And that the Kyrgyz who inhabited Talas
Had never lost it to a disputing foe,
Never yielded their companion to another,
And were a people unlike all others.
He heard that Üch-Koshoy, Talas, and broad Chatkal
Were their lands;
He heard that the dear folk dwelling there
Were his people.
When stirred, they hunted deer;
When they were not weary, they simply
Played freely at their ease.
He heard that those dear folk, the nation’s mainstay,
Were his people;
He heard that patterned carpets and ten kinds of cloth
Adorned their tethering lines.
He heard that Ala-Too, fairest of lands,
Was their mountain,
And that the fruit of this Ala-Too—
Aichürök, the woman taken as spoil—
Was his mother.
He heard the black giant’s account
That his people were Kyrgyz;
He heard the rough giant’s words
That he was fashioned differently.
The hero Manas was his grandfather,
And Semetey his own father.
He heard that in hilly Talas, in broad Keñ-Kol,
His village stood.
Never sated no matter how much he drank,
Never abandoning his ravenous desire,
When ridden through darkness
He prowled like a leopard;
Entered in a shooting contest, he brought good fortune;
Launched into battle, he equaled countless troops;
Once roused, he never missed his mark,
And none he struck survived.
Toward Külchoro’s side
She took the narrow shortcut,
Saying, “Pale-gray falcon, so full of spirit,
Well-born morning star,
Black-browed goshawk,”
And when she brought into the house
The young hero she had borne amid death,
Seytek, son of brave Semetey,
Was the very image of the gray-maned lion;
More than the hero himself,
He resembled the dark pupil of his eye.
He was like a prince who ruled a nation,
As though one scalp
Had been fitted over another,
As though the gray-maned lion had been born anew
And clothed in this form.
His front teeth gleamed white,
Like a chisel forged to shape stone;
When the boy charged,
He was a calamity to enemy warriors.
He roused himself like a tiger;
None who crossed blades with him survived.
Upon the champion’s two shoulders,
Two men seemed able to sit at once;
His two cheeks were prodigious,
As though they had sated two giants.
If Kyyaz and Kanchoro attacked,
He looked able to swallow them both.
Before the sweep of the boy’s blade,
Countless troops seemed to scatter in panic.
When enraged, he seemed able to trample
A hundred souls together, letting none escape.
To enemies who studied him,
His eyes seemed as vast as lakes,
As though they could suck out one’s soul.
Any person who beheld his majesty
Would lose his senses and flee;
Every single man
Would panic, unable to find a stratagem.
When a person looked upon his stature,
The mind of the beholder
Was scattered in astonishment.
His father, the gray-maned Semetey,
Seemed to stand there in his very form.
He was the precious legacy, dearer than life,
Truly left behind
By the gray-maned Manas himself.
Taking long strides together,
She led the young hero of noble blood
To your grieving Choro
And brought him to his side.
When Choro looked as the boy was led in,
He was like the gray-maned lion’s dark eye,
The very image of Semetey!
His chest was like a ravine;
His dear gleaming teeth
Were like tempered steel.
The breath from his mouth
Was like a wind across the mountain pass.
If this boy were roused,
He looked ready to devour the whole world.
His strength was extraordinary,
His courage beyond measure:
Such was the nature of the boy.
His lashes were flame, his eyes were embers;
No mortal ever held such wonder.
If he were merely stirred,
He looked ready to devour whoever fought him.
At the formidable boy, one looked
And said, “He is Semetey’s son.”
Glowing embers flew from him,
Blazing fire burst forth;
Among all the sons of humankind,
No such fierce one had ever arisen.
The formidable boy’s courage
And lionhearted valor—
His bravery took after his father.
He was like a champion who terrified nations,
Like a sovereign who ruled a people;
Could anyone who wrestled him survive?
The matchless champion—
The Creator who gives life
Had fashioned such a hero.
A black-mottled leopard,
He looked ready to rend flesh at once;
A compact, gray-maned lion,
With a fearsome tiger at his side—
No such being would soon appear again.
Behold his heroism:
If he charged straight ahead,
Sixty black camels
Could not match his hard courage and fierce wrath;
He looked able to wreak slaughter upon the Kalmyks
And take every one he met,
Letting not a soul escape.
Among mortal men,
All kinds are born.
Seen at his full height,
He was like a champion bearing a standard,
Like a commander ruling a nation.
His body was like a mountain ridge;
The boy’s mighty vigor
Was like the blast from a forge’s mouth.
The boy’s splendid form
Was like the crest of a high pass.
The sockets of his two eyes
Were like hollows in marshy water;
Whomever he charged, he looked ready
To seize, fold up, and swallow whole.
His broad, spacious forehead
Was like the sweeping slope of a mountain;
His stature seemed half a mountain—
Now Choro saw how splendidly he was formed.
When grieving Külchoro
Caught sight of the boy,
His whole body became glowing embers,
His eyes became burning fire;
Early words came only late,
And at the prince’s young son
He stared with eyes wide in wonder.
The boy was like the crest of a middle ridge;
If merely stirred,
He looked ready to devour whoever faced him.
He was a lion of heroic build,
A man who could subdue the whole world,
A warrior surpassing other men.
No one could measure himself against his strength;
In battle he looked ready to devour men.
He was hard as iron;
When he charged, he looked ready to devour a soul.
His body was like a planted plane tree;
The son of that peerless man
Could not rest without wreaking slaughter.
His surge was like the rush of a lake;
When he spoke at length, he flamed.
Fire poured from his mouth;
His sharpness showed
Like unyielding black steel.
He had the look of one who would advance
Against countless troops.
He had the look of one who would cast havoc
Upon all who grappled with him.
Subduing whoever challenged him,
Bringing disaster upon whoever fought him,
Throwing all who saw him into tumult—
Such havoc he seemed destined to wreak.
Not merely Kyyaz, but all the peoples,
The Chinese host and the hosts of Rum,
He looked destined to conquer.
Upon his enemies, he looked destined
To cast terror and turmoil.
He crouched like a lion;
If he faced those who came to blows with him,
He looked ready to slaughter them all.
His broad ears were like shields,
His bright eyes like morning stars—
Would any mortal dare face him?
Against the hero’s son,
Could anyone who faced him remain alive?
His body was straight as a plane tree.
Like a spring flowing from a ravine,
They stood face-to-face.
Overcome with love and yearning,
They melted into one another.
Any mortal who saw them rejoiced
As they swayed together like molten silver.
With a cry like a lion,
He pressed the boy to his breast, sobbing;
Külchoro’s head and limbs
Shook as he wailed.
“Are you the vision for which I prayed?
Are you the plane tree left by my elder?
You are all the vengeance left by the hero,
The mirror left by my lord.
Your elder has withered away like this,
Passing his days in servitude,
Drinking water through a reed.
I longed to die but could not die,
Could not take my own life,
Could not bring death upon myself.
When my hapless head endured
True misery and deepest humiliation,
I wandered long, burning and tormented.
My treasure left by my lord,
How long I have yearned to see you!
In my black, collared felt cloak,
When I went apart to gather firewood,
I met only suffering.
Abandoned to the enemy’s scorn,
The great ditch I dug became my lot;
Your elder grieved and was disgraced.
Though I sobbed, God would not take me;
